options.content:
**How to read this dashboard.** Charts count production code only, not tests, vendored or non-code files. Hover a title for what a chart measures and how to read it.
Change and entropy charts use the last 100 commits that touched code, read weekly; neighbouring points share most commits. The shaded band is a 95% confidence interval: movement inside it is noise. A dashed line at 1 marks chance: files are as far apart in the directory tree as at random.
Rows marked "(by language)" repeat the row above with one line per language. Complexity, non-local and dependency charts draw one line per language and a heavier one for all languages combined, which also moves when the language mix changes. A file's *reach* is the files it depends on through its imports and theirs.
No metric is validated against defects yet: read trends within this repository, not absolute values.

panels.title: Production code size
panels.description:
What: production code at each commit, in tokens (value) and files, and in tokens per language (c, rust, python, ecma); tests, vendored and non-code files excluded.

Read: context, not a score. A step marks a bulk commit, which often moves other charts too.

Trend: size is the strongest single predictor of defects: judge the other trends against it.

panels.title: Production code size (by language)
panels.description:
What: production code at each commit, in tokens (value) and files, and in tokens per language (c, rust, python, ecma); tests, vendored and non-code files excluded.

Read: context, not a score. A step marks a bulk commit, which often moves other charts too.

Trend: size is the strongest single predictor of defects: judge the other trends against it.

panels.title: Distance between files changed together (vs chance) ↓
panels.description:
What: how far apart in the directory tree the files changed by one commit are, relative to chance, over the last 100 code commits each week. Lower is better.

Read: 1 means changes pair up files as if at random; below 1, a commit's files sit close together. observed is the mean distance in directory steps (0: same directory, 2: sibling directories), expected its chance level. The shaded band is a 95% confidence interval for this average: movement inside it is noise.

Trend: rising means work spreads across the tree: what changes together does not live together. Change coupling correlates with defects.

panels.title: Rework within 7 days ↓
panels.description:
What: the share of edits to files already changed in the previous 7 days, over the last 100 code commits each week. Lower is better.

Read: 0.2 means a fifth of a typical commit's edits rework last week's code. Expect high values during feature work.

Trend: rising means code does not settle. A faster commit pace raises it too (see span_weeks). Unvalidated.

panels.title: File ownership by top author ↑
panels.description:
What: for files changed at least twice in the last 100 code commits, the share of changes made by their most active author, each week. Higher is better.

Read: 0.8 means a typical file's main author made 80% of its changes. The shaded band is a 95% confidence interval for this average: movement inside it is noise.

Trend: falling means more people change code nobody owns, which went with more defects (Bird et al.). Squash merges credit the merger.

panels.title: Work spread: effective files
panels.description:
What: over how many files the work of the last 100 code commits is effectively spread, each week; each commit counts once. Per language (c, rust, python, ecma): over how many of that language's files its share of the work is spread.

Read: 12 means as if spread evenly over 12 files. Files per commit is shown because bigger commits spread work by themselves.

Trend: rising means more places change at once. It predicted faults well in open-source projects (Hassan).

panels.title: Work spread: effective files (by language)
panels.description:
What: over how many files the work of the last 100 code commits is effectively spread, each week; each commit counts once. Per language (c, rust, python, ecma): over how many of that language's files its share of the work is spread.

Read: 12 means as if spread evenly over 12 files. Files per commit is shown because bigger commits spread work by themselves.

Trend: rising means more places change at once. It predicted faults well in open-source projects (Hassan).

panels.title: Encapsulated code share ↑
panels.description:
What: the share of function code in non-public functions (no pub, static, not exported, leading underscore), overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Higher is better.

Read: 0.6 means 60% of function code is internal. Visibility is written differently per language: compare each language over time, not languages with each other.

Trend: falling means the public surface grows faster than the code behind it.

panels.title: Duplicated code share ↓
panels.description:
What: the share of function code (functions of 50+ tokens) whose structure occurs more than once, ignoring names and literals, overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Lower is better.

Read: 0.05 means 5% of it has a structural twin.

Trend: rising means copy-paste instead of reuse. Whole-function clones only. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Code in large functions ↓
panels.description:
What: the share of function code in functions over 200 tokens, overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Lower is better.

Read: 0.5 means half of it sits in large functions. Compare each language over time.

Trend: rising means logic piles up in a few large functions. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Encapsulated code share (by language) ↑
panels.description:
What: the share of function code in non-public functions (no pub, static, not exported, leading underscore), overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Higher is better.

Read: 0.6 means 60% of function code is internal. Visibility is written differently per language: compare each language over time, not languages with each other.

Trend: falling means the public surface grows faster than the code behind it.

panels.title: Duplicated code share (by language) ↓
panels.description:
What: the share of function code (functions of 50+ tokens) whose structure occurs more than once, ignoring names and literals, overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Lower is better.

Read: 0.05 means 5% of it has a structural twin.

Trend: rising means copy-paste instead of reuse. Whole-function clones only. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Code in large functions (by language) ↓
panels.description:
What: the share of function code in functions over 200 tokens, overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Lower is better.

Read: 0.5 means half of it sits in large functions. Compare each language over time.

Trend: rising means logic piles up in a few large functions. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Decision points per function (90th percentile)
panels.description:
What: decision points (if, loops, match arms, catch, ternaries, &&, ||) per production function: the 90th percentile over functions (value), the most in one function (max), and the share of function code in functions with more than 10 (share).

Read: 6 means nine in ten functions have at most 6 decision points. A tail value, so adding simple code elsewhere does not lower it.

Trend: rising means the branchiest functions get branchier. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Nesting depth per function (90th percentile)
panels.description:
What: the deepest block below the function body, per production function: the 90th percentile over functions (value), the deepest function (max), and the share of function code in functions nested more than 3 deep (share).

Read: 2 means nine in ten functions nest at most two blocks below their body. Else-if chains stay flat.

Trend: rising means the most deeply nested functions get deeper. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Parameters per function (90th percentile)
panels.description:
What: parameters per production function (self included): the 90th percentile over functions (value), the most in one function (max), and the share of function code in functions with more than 5 (share).

Read: 4 means nine in ten functions take at most 4 parameters.

Trend: rising means wider interfaces: more to pass, more to understand at each call. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Decision points per 100 tokens
panels.description:
What: decision points (if, loops, match arms, catch, ternaries, &&, ||) per 100 production tokens, overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma).

Read: 5 means one decision every 20 tokens. Languages differ: compare each language over time, not languages with each other.

Trend: rising means more paths to understand and test per line. A density: adding plain code anywhere lowers it, and dividing by size does not remove size, so read function_decisions first. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Block nesting below function body
panels.description:
What: how many blocks deep function code sits below the function body, weighted by tokens, overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma); deep_share is the code in functions nested more than 3 deep.

Read: 1.5 means typical code is one to two blocks deep. Else-if chains stay flat.

Trend: rising means more conditions to keep in mind while reading. An average over all function code: read function_nesting first. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Global mutable state per 1,000 tokens
panels.description:
What: declarations of global mutable state per 1,000 production tokens (value), their number (count), overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma): Rust static mut, C/C++ file-scope variables, Python global, JS/TS module-level let and var.

Read: the forms differ: compare each language over time, not languages with each other.

Trend: rising means behaviour depends on more state outside the code in view. Read the count beside the density: adding plain code lowers the density without removing any state.

panels.title: Throws and panics per 1,000 tokens
panels.description:
What: non-local exits per 1,000 production tokens (value), their number (count), overall and per language (c, rust, python, ecma): throw, raise, Rust panics, unwrap and expect, C longjmp. invariants, unhandled and unfinished split them by intent.

Read: in Rust mostly unwrap and expect; elsewhere throws a distant caller must handle. Compare each language over time.

Trend: rising means control leaves functions in more places a caller cannot see. Read the count beside the density. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Stated invariants per 1,000 tokens
panels.description:
What: assertions that state what must hold, per 1,000 production tokens (value), and their number (count), overall and per language (c, rust, python): Rust assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!, their debug_ forms and unreachable!; Python assert; C/C++ assert().

Read: an invariant written down is checked where it is assumed. More is not worse: these panics are intended. Compare each language over time.

Trend: falling while the code grows means fewer assumptions are stated. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Fallible operations left unhandled per 1,000 tokens
panels.description:
What: Rust unwrap and expect calls per 1,000 production tokens (value), and their number (count).

Read: each one panics instead of handling a failure. Syntax cannot tell an unwrap that cannot fail (a fixed regex, a lock) from one that can, so this counts both.

Trend: rising means more failures turned into panics instead of handled. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Unfinished code per 1,000 tokens
panels.description:
What: markers of code left unfinished per 1,000 production tokens (value), and their number (count), overall and per language (rust, python): Rust todo! and unimplemented!, Python raise NotImplementedError.

Read: each panics when reached. Python's NotImplementedError also marks abstract methods, which are finished.

Trend: rising means more paths left for later. Unvalidated.

panels.title: goto per 1,000 C/C++ tokens
panels.description:
What: goto statements per 1,000 C/C++ tokens.

Read: mostly the goto-cleanup idiom, which is benign: watch spikes, not the level.

Trend: rising outside error cleanup means jumps that defeat top-to-bottom reading. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Share of its language's code a file depends on ↓
panels.description:
What: the share of the other files of its language that a typical production file depends on, through its imports and theirs (its reach), each week, per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Lower is better.

Read: 0.1 means a file depends on a tenth of its language's code. mean_reach and median_reach count files; largest_cycle is the largest group of files importing each other.

Trend: rising means a change anywhere can affect, and requires understanding, more of the code (MacCormack et al.).

panels.title: Distance imports reach (vs chance) ↓
panels.description:
What: how far through the directory tree imports reach, relative to chance, each week, per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Lower is better.

Read: 1 means imports reach as far as if rewired at random; below 1, files mostly import their neighbours. edges is the number of importing file pairs.

Trend: rising means code depends on code ever further away: the tree stops matching the structure. Moving files steps it.

panels.title: How complete the dependency metrics are, per language
panels.description:
What: the share of each language's imports of this repository's own code that codevitals could follow to a file, each week (c, rust, python, ecma).

Read: 1 means the dependency metrics see every import; 0.8 means they miss a fifth and read too low. fallback_share counts imports followed only to a crate root or __init__.py, which overstates reach.

Trend: a drop means the dependency metrics became less complete, not that the code changed.
